priorities.check_method: Standard-tier CHECK on the real diff. WHAT WAS FIXED: V6-0.2's tier banner, shipped S129 and marked DONE, could never render - its SCORE_TIER scan lived in HUD.sync, called at main.ts:2515, while effectsRenderer.sync does world.effects.length = 0 at main.ts:2486 (effectsRenderer.ts:73). I verified independently that each has exactly ONE call site and that nothing between lines 2486 and 2515 writes world.effects, so the loop always iterated ZERO entries in every mode for every player. It had passed CHECK because ui.tierBanner.test.ts pins only the pure arithmetic helpers and its own docblock concedes the draw path cannot be driven headlessly - testing everything EXCEPT the broken thing produced a confident green. FIX: split rather than relocate. drainTierBanner(world) is PUBLIC and called beside drainAudioEffects BEFORE effectsRenderer.sync; it owns the PLAYING guard, the watermark including the between-matches -1 reset, and the writes (text, fill, arming tierBannerFrames). animateTierBanner(world) stays private inside sync and owns the countdown, alpha and visible. The only field both touch is the non-PLAYING zeroing of tierBannerFrames, which is idempotent. captureTierBanner() was extracted as a new exported PURE function holding the effects scan plus the backward-tick guard - extracted specifically so the ORDERING is assertable without a Pixi Application, since the absence of that seam is precisely why S129 shipped blind. hud.sync was deliberately NOT relocated, because that would have required an argument about its order-independence relative to five other renderers whereas moving the SCAN out requires no such argument. VERIFICATION - and this is the material difference from S129, which could not verify the visual at all. rAF is still paused in a hidden Browser pane, but app.ticker.update() pumps the TRUE frame callback in PRODUCTION order, which sidesteps the blocker entirely. Driving it live in a dev page: the banner went ""/hidden -> 'TIER 1 - 500/1500' visible with alpha 1 and the effect's cyan fill; world.effects went 1 -> 0 in that SAME frame, which PROVES the drain read the effect before the wipe rather than merely being placed earlier in the source; it HELD on the next frame with no new effect (so the animate half owns the countdown and the drain's null-capture is inert); it HID at TITLE; and it RE-ARMED on the same tick next match with fill 0xFF0066, which proves the S129 watermark-reset fix survives the split. That last check specifically rules out the PRIME-AUDIT hazard that a careless split could produce a NEW never-renders variant - the drain latching text that never animates, or the animate running against a watermark the drain never advanced. THE GUARD WAS MUTATION-TESTED, not merely observed to pass: moving hud.drainTierBanner below the wipe makes ui.drainOrder.test.ts fail (1 failed / 8 passed), and reverting restores 9/9. A guard that only ever passes proves nothing. The suite also pins dedupe-by-tick, newest-tier-wins across a multi-tick drained batch, mixed-kind arrays, and watermark reset on a no-crossing frame. NUMBERS: tsc -b --noEmit exit 0 - npx vitest run 1941/1941 across 128 files (+9 tests, +1 file; baseline 1932/1932 across 127 was RE-RUN this session rather than inherited from the handoff) - npm run build exit 0, bundle 642.6/750 KiB with the delta MEASURED at +218 B against the 642.3 KiB baseline, 107.4 KiB headroom. reflexion_entries_to_archive.entry: V6-0.2 shipped a tier banner that could never render, and its test file was GREEN with ten passing tests. The tests pinned formatTierBanner, tierBannerAlpha and resetWatermarkIfRegressed - every pure helper AROUND the defect - while the defect itself was a call-site ORDERING fact: the scan ran 29 lines after the array it reads is emptied. The file's own docblock even recorded the reason for the gap ('the draw path cannot be driven headlessly'), so the blind spot was known and accepted rather than hidden. The lesson is that 'I extracted the logic into pure functions and pinned it' is NOT a substitute for verifying the wiring; it is a substitute for verifying the LOGIC, and those fail differently. When the untestable part is the part that decides whether the feature runs at all, extract a seam that makes the WIRING assertable - here, a source-order lock over main.ts plus a pure capture function whose order-sensitivity can be demonstrated. Both new guards target the call site; neither adds arithmetic coverage.

I wrote a source-order lock asserting that every world.effects consumer precedes the wipe in main.ts, and it passed on the first run. That proves nothing on its own - an assertion that can never fail is indistinguishable from one that always passes. So I mutated the source, moving hud.drainTierBanner below effectsRenderer.sync to reproduce the exact S129 arrangement, and confirmed the guard FAILED (1 failed / 8 passed), then reverted and confirmed 9/9. That took two minutes and converted 'the guard exists' into 'the guard bites'. This is the same principle as the prior session's lesson that when an artifact's job is to MEASURE, you must audit the measurement path - generalised: when an artifact's job is to CATCH, you must show it catching. Every regression lock should ship with evidence of a deliberate failure.

Two sessions running recorded 'the visual cannot be verified because a hidden Browser pane pauses requestAnimationFrame, so the Pixi ticker never advances' and substituted pure-function tests. That premise is true but the CONCLUSION was too broad: rAF is only the DRIVER of the ticker, not the ticker itself. app.ticker.update(now) pumps the real frame callback directly, in production order, with no rAF involved - so the whole 'is it wired correctly' question was answerable all along, and it is exactly the question that mattered. Pushing a genuine SCORE_TIER into world.effects and pumping one frame showed the banner arm, showed world.effects go 1 -> 0 in that same frame (proving the read beat the wipe rather than merely sitting earlier in the file), showed the hold, the hide at TITLE, and the re-arm next match. What genuinely remains blocked is much narrower than the recorded blocker: PIXEL output, because a hidden pane's GL context produces no frames. Lesson: when a capability is recorded as unavailable, re-derive WHICH layer is actually blocked before inheriting the conclusion - the blocked layer is often one level away from the layer you need.

Getting the approved PDR past the write gate exposed THREE independent bugs in the approval handshake, none previously visible. (1) validate_priority_id allows only [A-Za-z0-9_-], so a dotted id like P1-v06-0.3-... is rejected as malformed and glue_pdr_unlock returns without minting unlock_source; S129 used a dotted id too, so its unlock_source=user cannot have come from the hook and must have been hand-written. (2) The mint uses awk sub() on an EXISTING unlock_source line and cannot INSERT the key, so a priority entry lacking it makes the mint a silent no-op - while the hook still prints 'Cleared ... Edits permitted' UNCONDITIONALLY, so success and failure are indistinguishable from the output. (3) glue_pdr_unlock writes priority_state='unlocked' but pdca-final-gate.sh accepts only approved|in_progress|completed, i.e. the unlock hook writes a state its own gate rejects. Bug 2 is the dangerous one: I initially believed the mint had succeeded because the hook said so, and only caught it by reading the file back. Trust the STATE, not the announcement - and when a control claims to have acted, verify the artifact it was supposed to change.

MCV hard-failed because BACKLOG.md was modified with no absolute-path binding, and reading the verifier showed why my binding was ignored: line 289 collects verification[] ONLY from priorities whose status is 'completed'. The fastest fix would have been to mark the whole V6-0.3 priority completed - which would have been a lie, since the attribution work had not started, and precisely the fabrication class MCV exists to catch. The honest fix was to notice that the priority as recorded did not match reality: the banner repair genuinely WAS a complete, committed, independently revertable unit, and the attribution work genuinely was a separate not-started one. Splitting the record to match what actually happened made the checker pass as a side effect. When a gate blocks, the question to ask first is whether the gate has found a real misstatement in the bookkeeping - not how to phrase the claim so it slips through.

Two sessions recorded the banner's visual as unverifiable because the Browser pane will not composite. True, and not the whole board: the project already ships playwright, and headless Chromium composites fine. The blocked layer was the PANE, not the BROWSER. Before recording something as unverifiable, name the exact layer that is blocked and ask what else supplies it.

It was tempting to push a hand-built SCORE_TIER into world.effects to make the banner appear. Setting the leader's score to STEP-1 and letting scoring.ts emit costs the same and proves strictly more: the emitter's own gates (cinematicsEnabled, leaderId, newTier>oldTier) become part of the evidence. Same for the toast, driven through the app's live dispatchFn. A synthetic payload verifies the consumer while quietly assuming the producer.

My banner-presence check matched yellow pixels and reported ZERO hits across an entire hold sweep - because that run's leader was seat 1 (cyan) and the fill is the leader's colour. I nearly filed 'the banner does not render' off a detector measuring the wrong invariant. When an oracle returns all-negative, suspect the oracle before the subject.

The handoff said FULLY SPECCED, DO NOT RE-DERIVE, and that was right about the DESIGN. It was not a reason to skip Rule 21 on the plan's factual anchors: three did not hold - two renderers the PDR wanted in a 'reads world.effects' allowlist read no effects at all, a cited comment did not exist at the cited line, and a seven-arm table collapsed to one rule once the six dispatch sites were actually read. Do not re-derive the decision; do verify the state it rests on.

TIER_BANNER_FRAMES=120 reads like 2 seconds and is not: nothing caps the Pixi ticker, so it is 2.0s at 60Hz and ~0.83s at 144Hz. The owner was being asked to judge legibility 'in the ~2s hold' on hardware where it may be under a second. The new toast holds in SIM TICKS instead. When a window exists for a human to READ something, measure it in time, not frames.

The claim 'NO CI job runs vitest OR typecheck - zero hits across .github/workflows/' was carried by several handoffs, drove an owner ruling, and I repeated it in LOCKED_DECISIONS.md earlier in this same session. The grep was correct; the inference was half wrong, because npm run build IS 'tsc -b && vite build && check-bundle-size'. A literal-string search cannot see through a script indirection. When a grep is load-bearing for a decision, follow the scripts it names.

My first plate check compared with-plate against after-expiry and got a 22-pixel difference, which would have read as 'the plate never appeared'. The shot had landed inside the 0.3s fade-in. When a thing animates in, any measurement taken at t=0 measures the animation, not the thing. Sample in the steady state.

Adding a backing plate creates a new way to fail that the text alone did not have: the plate can outlive its label and sit on the board as a black rectangle. I wired visibility in the same statements on every path and then PROVED absence (0 -> 3759 -> 0 warm px) rather than only proving presence. Verifying that a feature appears is half a test.
